lesson.text: Quick memory: what are the four parts of fitness? (Stamina, strength, speed and flexibility.) Today: measuring your own fitness, and planning to improve it.
Fitness tests measure each part. Stamina: a bleep test or a timed run. Strength: sit-ups or press-ups in 30 seconds. Speed: a 20 m sprint. Flexibility: the sit and reach.
Make each test fair: warm up first, then do it the same way every time, in the same place, and measure carefully. Do it 3 times, and record your best result or the average.

Compare yourself with yourself. Your personal best is your best result so far. Everyone starts in a different place and improves at a different speed, so aim to beat your own score, not someone else's.
Set a SMART goal: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic and Time-bound. Not 'get fitter', but 'hold a plank for 60 seconds by the end of term'.
Make a plan: practise 3 times a week, adding a little each week, like 5 more seconds or 2 more skips. Keep a record in a table or a bar chart to see your progress.
Help your body improve: rest days let muscles recover and get stronger, and sleep, water and good food all help. If something hurts, stop and tell an adult.
Try it in the world: build a fitness trail with a sprint track and a plank mat. For real: choose one test, record your score, set a SMART goal, and test again in 4 weeks.

exercises.prompt: Match each fitness test to what it measures.
exercises.hint: What does each test ask your body to do?
exercises.explain: Sit and reach: flexibility. Sprint: speed. Bleep test: stamina. Press-ups: strength.

exercises.prompt: Your personal best is your best result so far.
exercises.explain: True: it is your own best so far, the score to beat next time.

exercises.prompt: Why should you warm up before a fitness test?
exercises.hint: What does a warm-up do to your muscles?
choices: to get your body ready and help stop injuries
exercises.explain: A warm-up gets your heart, muscles and joints ready, and helps stop injuries.

exercises.prompt: To see if you are improving, compare your score with your own last score.
exercises.hint: Everyone starts in a different place.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is a SMART goal?
exercises.hint: A SMART goal can be measured, and has a time.
choices: hold a plank for 60 seconds by half-term
be the best in the class
exercises.explain: 'Hold a plank for 60 seconds by half-term': it is specific, can be measured and has a time.

exercises.prompt: What makes a fitness test fair?
exercises.hint: What must stay the same to compare results?
choices: doing it the same way each time
doing it after a big meal
exercises.explain: Doing it the same way each time: then a better score really means you have improved.

exercises.hint: You need a starting score before you set a goal.
exercises.explain: Test and record, set a SMART goal, practise, then test again and compare.

exercises.prompt: Zara ran 20 m three times: 4.8 s, 4.6 s and 4.9 s. What is her best time, in seconds?
exercises.hint: In a race, is the best time the biggest number or the smallest?
exercises.explain: 4.6 s is the fastest, the smallest time: her personal best.

exercises.prompt: Rest days are wasted days for fitness.
exercises.hint: When do muscles recover and get stronger?
exercises.explain: False: muscles recover and get stronger on rest days, so rest is part of the plan.

exercises.hint: Is it about keeping going, or about pushing and holding?
exercises.explain: Stamina: a long run, the bleep test, swimming lengths. Strength: press-ups, a plank, squats.

exercises.prompt: The graph shows Bram's plank time each week. How many seconds longer was week 4 than week 1?
exercises.hint: Read week 1's bar and week 4's bar on the scale, then find the difference.
exercises.explain: Week 4: 50 seconds. Week 1: 20 seconds. 50 − 20 = 30 seconds longer.

exercises.prompt: Mimi can hold a plank for 40 seconds and adds 5 seconds each week. When will she reach 60 seconds?
exercises.hint: How many more seconds, and how many lots of 5 is that?

exercises.prompt: After 3 weeks, Tilly's sit and reach has not improved. What is the best thing to do?
exercises.hint: Plans can be improved, just like designs.
choices: look at the plan, change it and keep going
practise 10 times a day, however it feels
exercises.explain: Look at the plan, change it (a new stretch, more often), and keep going. Progress can take time.

exercises.prompt: Getting fitter usually takes weeks of practice, not days.
exercises.hint: How quickly do muscles and hearts change?
exercises.explain: True: bodies improve little by little, over weeks, so keep going and keep a record.

exercises.prompt: Bram's three standing long jumps were 150 cm, 156 cm and 159 cm. What is the mean (the average), in cm?
exercises.hint: Add the three jumps, then share the total by 3.

exercises.prompt: What is the most useful way to see your progress over a term?
exercises.hint: What lets you look back and compare?
choices: record every test in a table or a chart
only look at your first test
exercises.explain: A table or a bar chart of every test shows your progress clearly.
